title: Caching Basics
subtitle: Watch one hot record get read and written through a cache, and see how each policy trades speed, freshness, and safety.
learn: How cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-back, and write-around differ
How hit ratio turns into average latency and database load
How LRU and LFU choose what to throw out when the cache is full
Where caches live between the browser and the database

steps.title: The same row, ten thousand times
steps.body: Your product page reads the same few popular rows again and again. Assume 10,000 reads per second, a database read that takes about 10 ms, and a cache read that takes about 1 ms. With no cache, every read hits the database, so it carries all 10,000 queries per second. Most of that work is repeated answers, and a cache is a small fast store that remembers them.
steps.idea: A cache trades a little memory and some freshness risk for far fewer slow reads.
steps.caption: Every read goes to the database.

steps.title: Cache-aside: the app does the work
steps.body: In cache-aside (also called lazy loading) the application code owns the logic. It asks the cache first. On a miss it reads the database, then stores the result in the cache with a time limit (TTL) for next time. This first read is slower, about 11 ms, because it pays for both lookups.
steps.idea: Cache-aside fills the cache on demand, so only data that is actually read gets cached.
steps.caption: Miss: the app falls back to the database, then fills the cache.

steps.title: A hit, and why the ratio matters
steps.body: The next read finds the key in the cache and returns in about 1 ms with no database work. Hit ratio is hits divided by total reads. At 90% with 1 ms hits and 11 ms misses, average latency is 0.9 x 1 + 0.1 x 11 = 2 ms, and the database sees only 1,000 reads per second instead of 10,000. Going from 90% to 99% cuts database reads by another 10 times.
steps.idea: Small gains in hit ratio near the top cut database load sharply, because misses are what you pay for.
steps.caption: Hit: served from memory, database untouched.

steps.title: Read-through: the cache loads itself
steps.body: Read-through hides the miss logic. The app only ever talks to the cache. If the key is absent, the cache itself fetches from the database, stores the value, and returns it. The behavior matches cache-aside, but the loading code lives in one place (the cache layer or library) instead of in every caller. Plain Redis does not do this itself; a library or caching layer sits in front and does the loading.
steps.idea: Read-through and cache-aside differ in who loads on a miss: the cache or the application.
steps.caption: The cache fetches from the database on a miss.

steps.title: Write-through: update both, then confirm
steps.body: On a write, write-through updates the cache and then the database in one operation, and only acknowledges once both succeed. Reads that go through the cache stay in step with committed data, and nothing is lost on a cache crash. A failed database write must also fail or undo the cache update. The price is that every write waits for the slower database, and you may cache values nobody reads again.
steps.idea: Write-through buys consistency and durability by making each write as slow as the database.
steps.caption: The write reaches the database before the app is told it worked.

steps.title: Write-back: acknowledge now, save later
steps.body: Write-back (write-behind) updates only the cache, acknowledges immediately, and flushes dirty entries (values changed in the cache but not yet saved to the database) to the database later in batches. Writes become very fast and many updates to one key collapse into a single database write. The danger is that if the cache node dies before a flush, those acknowledged writes are gone, unless the cache persists or replicates them.
steps.idea: Write-back is the fastest write path, and the only one that can lose data you already acknowledged.
steps.caption: Fast ack from the cache; the database catches up asynchronously.

steps.title: Write-around: skip the cache on writes
steps.body: Write-around sends writes straight to the database and leaves the cache alone. It suits data that is written once and rarely read soon after, such as uploaded logs or a bulk import, because it keeps them from filling the cache. The catch is that the first read after a write is a miss, and an old cached copy of that key is stale until it expires or is removed.
steps.idea: Write-around protects the cache from write-heavy, read-light data at the cost of a cold first read.
steps.caption: The write goes to the database only.

steps.title: The cache is full: who goes?
steps.body: Memory is limited, so a full cache must evict something to admit a new key. LRU (least recently used) removes the key untouched the longest, betting that recent use predicts future use. LFU (least frequently used) removes the key with the fewest accesses, which protects long-term favorites. LRU is simple and widely used (Redis offers it as allkeys-lru, but it must be configured); a one-time bulk scan can flush hot keys out of it, which LFU resists. LFU can keep once-popular keys too long unless counts decay.
steps.idea: Eviction is a bet about the future: LRU bets on recency, LFU bets on popularity.
steps.caption: Cache is full: SET new key evicts an old one.

steps.title: Caches live in layers
steps.body: A request can be answered at many points. The browser caches files and responses, a CDN (content delivery network) edge serves popular content near the user and forwards misses to the app, its origin server, the app may hold a small in-process cache, a shared cache like Redis (an in-memory key-value store) serves all app servers, and the database keeps hot pages in its own memory. Closer to the user is faster, but harder to keep consistent and to clear.
steps.idea: Put each cache as close to the user as the data's freshness rules allow.
steps.caption: The CDN and the shared cache answer before the database; the browser cache is checked first.

steps.title: Pick the policy by the data
steps.body: Read side: cache-aside keeps logic in the app, read-through moves it into the cache. Write side: write-through is safe and slower, write-back is fast and risky, write-around keeps the cache clean of write-only data. Track hit ratio, since it sets both latency and database load, and pick an eviction policy that matches your access pattern. Common pairings: cache-aside + write-around (delete the key on update), read-through + write-through. Keeping cached copies correct over time is covered in the invalidation lesson.
steps.idea: Choose read and write policies per data type, then watch the hit ratio.
steps.caption: Five policies, one goal: fewer slow reads.

quiz.q: Cache hits take 1 ms and misses take 11 ms (cache check plus database read). With an 80% hit ratio, what is the average read latency?
quiz.why: Average = 0.8 x 1 + 0.2 x 11 = 0.8 + 2.2 = 3 ms. Only 20% of reads are misses, but they cost 11x a hit, so they supply 2.2 of the 3 ms.

quiz.q: A counter service acknowledges each increment from the cache and flushes to the database every few seconds. The cache server crashes. What is the realistic loss?
options: Nothing, the database always has every write first
The increments not yet flushed, even though they were acknowledged
quiz.why: This is write-back. Unflushed dirty entries live only in the cache, so a crash loses writes the client was told succeeded.

quiz.q: A nightly report reads 5 million rows exactly once, alongside normal traffic. Which cache behavior is most at risk?
options: LRU, because the scan makes one-time keys look recently used and pushes hot keys out
LFU, because scan keys get high counts and push out hot keys
Cache-aside TTL, because scans shorten the TTL
None, since eviction ignores access order
quiz.why: LRU treats every just-read key as valuable, so a big scan evicts the genuinely popular keys. LFU keeps frequently used keys and resists this.

quiz.q: Which data is the best fit for write-around?
options: A user's shopping cart read on every page
A feature flag read by every request
A session token checked on each call
Audit log rows that are written constantly and rarely read back
quiz.why: Write-around avoids filling the cache with data unlikely to be read soon. The cart, flag, and session are read-heavy and belong in the cache.

cheatsheet.def: App checks the cache, on a miss reads the database and fills the cache itself. Most common pattern; only requested data gets cached.
App talks only to the cache; the cache loads missing keys from the database. Same effect as cache-aside, loading logic lives in the cache layer.
Write goes to cache and database together before the ack. Consistent and durable, but writes are as slow as the database.
Write updates only the cache and flushes to the database later. Fastest writes, but unflushed data is lost if the cache fails.
Write goes straight to the database, skipping the cache. Good for write-once, rarely read data; first read afterward is a miss.
Hits divided by total reads. Average latency = hit% x hit time + miss% x miss time; database load = misses per second.
LRU evicts the least recently used key; LFU evicts the least frequently used. LRU is simple but vulnerable to scans; LFU protects steady favorites.
